articles.title: Ring upgraded its peephole doorbell camera to 2K
articles.summary: Ring’s new Peephole Cam 2K smart doorbell camera gets a big resolution upgrade and a price drop to $100.
articles.body: Ring has debuted a new version of its smart doorbell camera that’s designed to be easily installed as a replacement for a door’s peephole without drilling or running wires. The Peephole Cam 2K is a replacement for the brand’s Door View Cam that first debuted in 2019 and, alongside a sleeker design, it features a bump from 1080P to 2K video recording, some tracking upgrades, and a cheaper price. It’s available for preorder now for $99.99 with shipping expected later this month. As with previous models, the Peephole Cam 2K is divided into two halves that connect to each other through your door’s peephole. On the outside there’s a camera, doorbell, speaker, and microphone, while inside are additional electronics including a removable battery good for an estimated 120 days of use between charges. But there’s no preview screen on the inside, so to check who’s at your door you’ll need to reach for your phone or a compatible smart display. [Image: The two halves of the camera connect through a door’s peephole, so no drilling or complicated wiring is required. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ring2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] That inconvenience is potentially outweighed by being able to see and respond to whoever’s at your door from anywhere, even when you’re not at home. The Peephole Cam 2K will also deliver real-time motion alerts with brief descriptions of what its camera is seeing, and you can limit its motion detection to specific regions of its wide-angle 140-degree field-of-view so that passing cars, for example, don’t trigger alerts. However, features like being able to review recorded events for up to 180 days and specific alerts for detected packages are only available with an additional Ring Protect plan.

articles.title: Google says hackers are calling financial firm employees to hack and extort victims | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Groups of hackers are breaking into large U.S. financial firms to steal sensitive data and extort victims, Google’s security researchers report.
articles.body:
Even in the age of AI-powered autonomous cyberattacks , the crude, tried and tested hacking techniques of tricking victims into doing things they shouldn’t are still producing great results.

Groups of unknown hackers are targeting and breaking into large financial and investment firms in the United States with the goal of stealing sensitive data to extort the victims with the threat of publishing it, Google’s security researchers wrote in a report on Thursday.

The company did not name the victims, but Reuters reported that among them there are leading private equity firms such as Apollo Global Management, Bain Capital, Blackstone, Bridgewater Associates, CME Group, KKR, Moody’s, and TPG.

The hacking groups, which Google dubbed Falcon, Helix, Pink, and Redact, are using an old-fashioned technique to break into those firms: phone calls to employees’ personal cellphones in which the hackers pretend to be co-workers or IT helpdesk staffers, during which they try to trick targets into entering their credentials and multi-factor codes on spoofed websites, according to Google. In cybersecurity parlance, this technique is known as voice phishing, or vishing.

Some of the groups identified by Google run websites where they publicize their hacks and threaten to leak the stolen data as a way to extort the victims into paying a ransom, a common strategy among cybercriminals.

“We conduct every negotiation on professional terms. The publication of your data is never our preferred resolution; it is the consequence of refusal to engage, deliberate stalling, or failure to honor an agreement,” read one of the sites. “Respond promptly and in good faith, and the matter is resolved without further incident.”

Google researchers said that the different groups may all be part of a larger umbrella collective the company tracks under the name UNC6671. But it’s unclear if they are affiliates, splinter groups, or they all use the same Phishing-as-a-Service infrastructure.

“We believe that this most likely reflects a coordinated group of threat actors operating multiple public extortion brands possibly in an effort to compartmentalize operations, hide overall breach volumes, and isolate any negotiation fallout,” read the report.

According to Google, the hacking groups have also previously targeted large companies in the manufacturing, real estate, healthcare, and insurance sectors, as well as tech, transportation, and hospitality companies with the goal of stealing “valuable intellectual property, software source code, or sensitive VIP client data.”

More recently, the hackers have targeted legal and financial organizations such as private equity firms. “Concentrating on organizations involved in mergers, acquisitions, capital deployment, and litigation may reflect a strategy to target high-value corporate and confidential data to maximize leverage extortion demands,” wrote Google’s researchers.

Google said that one cryptocurrency wallet associated with one of the hacking groups received around $10 million in bitcoin in the first few months of this year, and that the hackers usually demand from $750,000 to $3 million from victims.

Laurie Bischel, a spokesperson for CME Group, declined to comment.

Apollo Global Management, Bain Capital, Blackstone, Bridgewater Associates, KKR, Moody’s, and TPG did not respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Google's top hacker hunter explains why hacking groups get code names | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Google recently changed how it refers and assigns names to hacking groups. TechCrunch spoke with one of the world’s foremost experts on tracking hackers to understand why companies give hackers codenames.
articles.body:
For more than a decade, the cybersecurity industry has been assigning names to different hacking groups. Some of them, like Fancy Bear , have crossed over into the mainstream because of their prominent hacks and memorable names. Others are only known within the cybersecurity industry.

Oftentimes, even industry insiders can’t keep track. In part, that’s because every company names hacking groups differently. That’s why there are resources like this one , which attempt to be a one-stop shop where cybersecurity professionals, government officials, policymakers, journalists, and the wider public can make sense of who is who.

Last month, Google became the latest company to revamp its naming system for hacking groups.

Gone are the days of APT1, APT41, or APT whatever number , which was the system adopted by Mandiant, once an independent security firm that’s now part of Google. Mandiant was the first to adopt a naming scheme.

From now on, Google’s system is relatively simple: A hacking group will have a first name that is memorable and random, and a second word whose initial indicates the country of origin: Castle for China, Ion for Iran, Neptune for North Korea, and Relic for Russia.

According to Shane Huntley, the chief technology officer of Google Threat Intelligence Group, the company’s in-house hacker hunting team, the revamp was necessary to bring clarity to security researchers both inside the company and externally.

In the early 2010s, when companies started publishing reports on cyberattacks and naming the hackers behind them, Huntley told TechCrunch, “We were not expecting to have as many threat groups as we do today.”

It became hard to keep track of everyone. Google now tracks more than 5,000 “activity clusters” in several countries, according to John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google Threat Intelligence Group. Huntley said that there are very few developed nations that don’t have their own cyber capabilities and hacking groups.

But what is the point of naming hacking groups? It’s not just an academic exercise, Huntley explained. The goal is to have a baseline understanding of who is attacking who, and how they are attacking them. That way organizations can recognize threats more quickly, prepare against them, and ideally stop them, or at least investigate incidents more promptly.

All that, he said, is possible only if you name the hackers and track them consistently.

“If you actually get hacked by them or you’re dealing with some incident, knowing how that actor behaves, what they do, what they’ve done in the past, all of these details become critically important to help the response and also work out your coverage against these threats as well,” said Huntley.

Knowing how the North Korean government hackers known as the Lazarus Group behave, what their goals usually are, and who they work for gives defenders a starting point in dealing with these hackers.

Tracking state-sponsored hackers, while challenging, is easier than tracking cybercriminal groups and hackers-for-hire, Huntley explained. The government hackers tend to have more consistent targets and activities, while cybercriminal groups have members that come and go, sometimes splinter, and otherwise are more amorphous. Hacker-for-hire groups and spyware makers tend to have a lot of customers in different parts of the world, making them slightly harder to track.

A common criticism whenever a new naming system gets announced is: Why don’t all companies and organizations just use the same code names? While that seems like an easy question to answer, the reality is that every company has a slightly different view of every group, based on their own sets of data and telemetry. Huntley said this is an inescapable reality that can’t be avoided just by sharing more information among companies and groups of researchers.

“No one has perfect visibility,” he said. “We are building our model and our best understanding, but we will never know everything about what’s going on.”

By unifying the naming scheme of Google’s old Threat Analysis Group, which Huntley headed, and Mandiant, at least now there’s one fewer scheme to remember. For everything else, refer to this gargantuan list .

articles.title: Brendan Carr is one firing away from an unchecked FCC
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s nomination of Republican Danielle Thumann Severs to the Federal Communications Commission raises questions about the agency’s rules.
articles.body: President Donald Trump already holds a Republican majority in the agency tasked with regulating America’s communications systems. But with a new nomination to the Federal Communications Commission, he could move to shut out opposing voices altogether — albeit at a legal risk. The FCC is currently composed of two Republicans and one Democrat — Republican Chair Brendan Carr and Commissioner Olivia Trusty, and Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez. This mixed group gives the agency a three-member quorum that allows it to vote on major actions, though it still falls short of the five members (no more than three from a single party) the FCC is meant to have. But late last week, Trump nominated a third Republican, Carr adviser Danielle Thumann Severs. If she’s confirmed, it won’t change the basic math of which policies win votes. But it would mean there’s a quorum even without Gomez. That could open the door to Trump firing the FCC’s lone Democrat, something she herself has wondered why he hasn’t already done. Gomez may not have much hard power in the current FCC, but her removal would be a blow to the public interest. Commissioners often have access to information that the public might not otherwise know about, and can raise nonconfidential issues in their public dissents and statements. And even in situations where dissenting voices are overruled, they can push the majority to offer more robust reasoning in their decisions. During the Trump administration, Gomez has used her post to call attention to FCC actions she thinks violate the First Amendment, and pushed back on policies loosening broadcast consolidation rules. Even with Gomez in place, Carr’s FCC has threatened broadcasters over programming they air under seldom-used rules, approved a major broadcast merger by waiving policies set by Congress, and banned Roombas.  Trump could well be able to remove Gomez, given that he fired the Federal Trade Commission’s two Democrats without cause and got away with it. Like the FTC, the FCC was created as an independent agency, with a bipartisan panel of staggered terms that would supposedly insulate it from a given administration’s whims. But under the unitary executive theory, which Trump allies including Carr and FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson endorse, all power held by them belongs to the president. The Supreme Court’s ruling affirming Trump’s ability to fire the FTC’s Democrats bolstered this. But there are still good reasons Trump could spare Gomez, particularly that firing her could put the FCC’s legitimacy in question, as former FCC senior staffer Blair Levin writes. Even after SCOTUS legitimized the FTC firings, the Communications Act’s language grants the FCC unique quirks. It could provide stronger legal ground to argue that one party can’t hold all the seats on the panel, Levin adds, and a court could determine it is more like the Federal Reserve, insulated from presidential firings, than the FTC.  Gomez’ term is technically lapsed, but she can stay on until the end of 2027 unless her seat is filled sooner, or she’s renominated. With limited Senate floor time ahead of the midterm elections and key Democrats’ opposition to confirming a Republican nominee without a Democratic one, the FCC could remain in a holding pattern for quite some time.

articles.title: ‘That is not acceptable’: Judge orders Google to make rival app store installs easier
articles.summary: Judge James Donato just ordered Google to make it easier to install rival app stores on Android.
articles.body: One month after Epic Games and Google seemingly stopped fighting over the future of Android app distribution, they were back in a San Francisco courtroom today — where Judge James Donato just ordered Google to make it easier to install rival app stores on Android. It’s been nearly three years since a jury unanimously decided that Google had an illegal monopoly over Android apps, and almost two years since Judge Donato decided the best way of undoing that monopoly would be to crack open Android app distribution. Donato ordered Google to carry rival Android app stores inside its own Google Play Store, and to provide rivals with complete access to Google’s full catalog of apps, for several years. But Epic argued that Google is still making it too difficult to install rival app stores, showing the entire courtroom a live demo of how many steps it currently takes — and Judge Donato agreed that some of those steps were unnecessary “anticompetitive friction” and ordered Google to remove them. First, Epic’s lawyer Yonatan Even showed that if you search Google’s Play Store for the term “store for apps,” no third-party app stores appear, only physical stores. “Wait, why did Walmart come up?” Judge Donato asked. “That’s not good,” he exclaimed. [Image: These are my own screenshots, not the live demo shown in court, as no photography is allowed there. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/app-store-changes-google-play.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] “That is not acceptable, that has to be fixed. I want every possible variation that’s even only 70 percent properly phrased,” Donato ordered. Google’s counsel agreed to make it happen. Similarly, Judge Donato bristled when he saw that users have to press a “view” button before they can press an “install” button when choosing to install a third-party app store, and so that will change too. “You don’t get that when you’re looking at Apple Music,” he noted. “Make that install, not view,” Donato ordered, and Google agreed to do so. Later, Epic showed that when you search for “app store,” or even if you search directly for Aptoide, the first rival store to make it into the Google Play Store, Google doesn’t surface a normal list of apps — it shows you a new banner you have to click through to a dedicated third-party app store page. That’s not just a problem for brand-new app stores, argued Even. Big, established companies like Amazon might decide not to launch app stores because they’d be losing the ability to appear in normal app store search results. Judge Donato ordered Google to fix that one, too, telling the company that it didn’t make any sense. “Why doesn’t it say ‘are you looking for music’ when you type in ‘music store’?” he asked. Google’s attorney replied that Epic and Google had already agreed that app stores are a special category of apps that have advanced permissions. But Donato said the warning on the third-party app store page itself was sufficient to address that — there’s no need to ask a user whether they really want the thing they searched for, whether it’s a game store or a glass of water. “We all know that when you go to a Google store or an Apple store and you type in the name of your app, you’re going to get one thing you were looking for and 10 things you don’t want,” said the judge, explaining that he doesn’t think average users will be confused when they get what they’re asking for. “Take off the ‘are you looking for’ screen, there’s no purpose for that. There’s a friction there that has no purpose whatsoever,” Donato said. The judge wants these changes fast. “Have it done by a week from today,” he told Google. “If there’s some problem with that, let me know.‘

It’s been nearly three years since a jury unanimously decided that Google had an illegal monopoly over Android apps, and almost two years since Judge Donato decided the best way of undoing that monopoly would be to crack open Android app distribution. Donato ordered Google to carry rival Android app stores inside its own Google Play Store, and to provide rivals with complete access to Google’s full catalog of apps, for several years. But Epic argued that Google is still making it too difficult to install rival app stores, showing the entire courtroom a live demo of how many steps it currently takes — and Judge Donato agreed that some of those steps were unnecessary “anticompetitive friction” and ordered Google to remove them. First, Epic’s lawyer Yonatan Even showed that if you search Google’s Play Store for the term “store for apps,” no third-party app stores appear, only physical stores. “Wait, why did Walmart come up?” Judge Donato asked. “That’s not good,” he exclaimed. [Image: These are my own screenshots, not the live demo shown in court, as no photography is allowed there. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/app-store-changes-google-play.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] “That is not acceptable, that has to be fixed. I want every possible variation that’s even only 70 percent properly phrased,” Donato ordered. Google’s counsel agreed to make it happen. Similarly, Judge Donato bristled when he saw that users have to press a “view” button before they can press an “install” button when choosing to install a third-party app store, and so that will change too. “You don’t get that when you’re looking at Apple Music,” he noted. “Make that install, not view,” Donato ordered, and Google agreed to do so. Later, Epic showed that when you search for “app store,” or even if you search directly for Aptoide, the first rival store to make it into the Google Play Store, Google doesn’t surface a normal list of apps — it shows you a new banner you have to click through to a dedicated third-party app store page. That’s not just a problem for brand-new app stores, argued Even. Big, established companies like Amazon might decide not to launch app stores because they’d be losing the ability to appear in normal app store search results. Judge Donato ordered Google to fix that one, too, telling the company that it didn’t make any sense. “Why doesn’t it say ‘are you looking for music’ when you type in ‘music store’?” he asked. Google’s attorney replied that Epic and Google had already agreed that app stores are a special category of apps that have advanced permissions. But Donato said the warning on the third-party app store page itself was sufficient to address that — there’s no need to ask a user whether they really want the thing they searched for, whether it’s a game store or a glass of water. “We all know that when you go to a Google store or an Apple store and you type in the name of your app, you’re going to get one thing you were looking for and 10 things you don’t want,” said the judge, explaining that he doesn’t think average users will be confused when they get what they’re asking for. “Take off the ‘are you looking for’ screen, there’s no purpose for that. There’s a friction there that has no purpose whatsoever,” Donato said. The judge wants these changes fast. “Have it done by a week from today,” he told Google. “If there’s some problem with that, let me know.‘

articles.title: Apple and Epic argue over how much Apple should get from purchases made outside the App Store
articles.summary: Apple’s new App Store proposal would allow it to collect fees from developers on digital purchases made via external links, including a 15 percent cut from standard apps.
articles.body: In a new filing in its long-running legal dispute with Epic Games, Apple has proposed a structure that would allow it to collect fees on digital purchases made via external links that don’t use the company’s in-app purchase system. Epic has already responded, saying that Apple’s request is “far outside of the bounds” of the court’s guidance. Right now, Apple cannot take a commission on external purchases after California district court judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in April 2025 that the company “willfully” didn’t comply with her 2021 Epic Games v. Apple injunction. However, a Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel said that Apple should be able to charge a commission based on “necessary costs,” and Apple shared its proposal for fees in Thursday’s filing. (The Supreme Court has also said it will hear arguments about whether Apple willfully violated the April 2025 ruling.) Under Apple’s proposal, it would collect: * 15 percent of fees from purchases in “standard apps” * 10 percent of fees for apps in the Video Partner Program, the News Partner Program, the Mini Apps Partner Program, and subscription renewals * 5 percent of fees from apps in the Small Business Program However, Apple says its “necessary costs” to allow external purchases, as defined by the Ninth Circuit, “would be essentially zero.” The company argues that, based on an “expert analysis,” at the proposed rates, “it appears that large numbers of U.S. developers collectively accounting for the lion’s share of App Store revenue will be able to link out profitably.” Apple also says the rates would let it recoup “at least some compensation” for its tools, technologies, and services it provides to developers. Here’s Epic’s statement in reply to the filing: > Apple’s filing is in, and Apple admitted that under the Ninth Circuit’s definition of “necessary costs” they would charge 0% for purchases made via linkouts to the web. > Apple proposed linkout fees of 15% for standard apps and 5% for Small Business Program apps. Epic believes these fees are far outside of the bounds of the Ninth Circuit’s guidance on permissible fees, and we have roughly 60 days to file our opposition supported by expert witnesses.

articles.title: Trump declares 100 percent tariffs on many drones and all aircraft parts
articles.summary: President Trump has declared a whopping 100 percent tariff on imports of drones with thermal cameras, drones weighing over 25kg (57 pounds), and any kind of part for any kind of aircraft weighing over 25kg.
articles.body: The United States has already banned future foreign drones from entering the United States unless their companies kiss the ring — as well as routers, robots, and Roombas. Now, President Donald Trump is targeting existing drone imports and parts, too. He’s going to try to make them cost a lot more. In a presidential action, he’s declared a whopping 100 percent tariff on imports of drones with thermal cameras, drones weighing over 25kg (57 pounds), and any kind of part for any kind of unmanned aircraft weighing over 25kg — you can read the full list here. For all other drones, including tiny sub-250-gram “Mini” consumer drones, he’s declared a 25 percent tariff. In Trump fashion, these tariffs have a huge loophole: If a company commits to making some of their drones or aircraft parts in the United States, they don’t have to pay tariffs. Trump suggested he’d make similar deals when he threatened a 100 percent tariff on computer chips last year. And Trump is giving the EU, Japan, Liechtenstein, South Korea, Switzerland, and Taiwan a lower rate of 15 percent, and a rate of 10 percent for the UK, “provided that substantially all hardware, software, and technology originates from within these countries and the United States.” Stated reasons for the new tariffs include: * “many U.S. commercial manufacturers that produce UAS domestically are highly dependent on foreign sources for critical UAS components, such as motors, electronic speed controllers, lithium-ion batteries, and docking stations, which creates unacceptable national security vulnerabilities.” * “products pose an information technology security risk because their software allows data to be sent back to the manufacturer in a foreign country.” * “there are concerns as to whether the U.S. industry can produce UAS and UAS components at the required speed and scale to adequately support national security operations and activities, including during a surge for wartime or armed conflict, or in a manner to sustain long-term economic competitiveness.” Trump is also dangling a carrot, not just wielding a stick. The proclamation states that he’s authorizing the Secretary of Commerce to create a new program “to incentivize new investment in U.S. production facilities to produce UAS and UAS components.” That could be interesting, but last we checked, the government’s drone incentives were aimed toward drones for war. The Supreme Court already ruled earlier this year that Trump’s global tariffs were illegal; the US Court of International Trade ruled against them too, though Trump continues to announce more. As of today, it appears that Trump’s tariffs are enriching corporate America at the expense of everyday citizens. First, companies raise their prices so that you pay the cost of tariffs instead of them. Then, those companies get gigantic refunds from the government when the tariffs are declared illegal. Finally, they profit. Companies do not pass those refunds along to you, even though you paid for them, and they do not lower their prices either. The tariffs aren’t the US government’s only attempt to target larger foreign drones in the US. The FCC recently threatened to retroactively ban “military-grade” drones using definitions that would also catch drones for farmers, first responders, and light shows in the same net.

articles.title: Judge orders Kalshi to shut down most of its bets in Washington.
articles.summary:
A preliminary injunction issued Wednesday finds the prediction market has likely broken state laws against running an illegal gambling operation.
Washington State AG Nick Brown:
> The order requires Kalshi to stop offering, accepting, or facilitating wagers on sports, elections, politics, entertainment, culture, tech and science, or mentions in Washington. Kalshi must implement an IP address and residency based geofence by August 19 and a multi-source geofencing solution by September 2.
> This does not include all the wagers offered on Kalshi, but it includes a substantial part of their business, which in recent years has been increasingly driven by sports wagers.

articles.title: When housing is unaffordable, this artist’s device makes pedaling harder
articles.summary: Brooklyn-based artist Justin Blinder created a device that illustrates how soaring housing costs are making life in the city that much harder.
articles.body: Justin Blinder had just been laid off when he first came up with the idea for Ground Truth. It was 2020, two weeks before covid lockdown went into effect, and the Brooklyn-based artist and technologist had no idea what the future would hold. He started working for the food delivery apps, and as he was riding his bike across the city, he began noticing the stark differences between neighborhoods. “I really started to kind of become a bit more aware of how different neighborhoods, often right next to each other, could feel very economically and psychologically very far apart, even though it’s just really within close proximity,” he said. “And also just how those inequalities can sometimes feel quite unusually physical. A lot of times higher elevation can contribute to the desirability and cost of a neighborhood through better views and lower flood exposure.” These observations led him to think about the relationship between the food he was delivering, the neighborhoods it was going to, the buildings he encountered, and even the expectations he developed about potential tips. “All that kind of culminated into this sort of line of thinking that led to Ground Truth that had been percolating after that for a few years,” Blinder said. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ground-truth-device-connection.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ground-truth-device-field-04.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ground-truth-device-03.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ground-truth-device-02.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Ground Truth, Blinder’s new art project, is a small gray box that attaches to the front fork of a bike and changes the physical difficulty of riding according to the housing affordability of the surrounding neighborhood. When housing is more affordable, pedaling becomes easier. But when a rider enters an area where housing costs consume a larger proportion of residents’ incomes, the bike’s resistance increases, making the rider work harder. “And so it’s really thinking about how to take economic abstractions in this case, really the affordability of cost-of-living prices, and turn them from something that really reduces people to numbers and brings it back into more of a direct physical experience that’s rooted in reality and in the streets,” he said. After abandoning some early ideas for fear of unexpected legal consequences, Blinder settled on building an external mechanism that would allow him to affect the bike without penetrating its closed electronic systems. Using a Citi Bike as his “canvas,” he noticed that the front drum-brake mechanism was physically exposed. When the rider pulls the front brake handle, a lever on the front fork moves to apply pressure. He realized he could build a wireless mechanism that attaches to this lever and effectively acts as an additional brake actuator, allowing the device to increase or decrease the bike’s resistance. The hardware itself is relatively simple, consisting of an ESP32-S3 microcontroller, a GPS module, a high-torque servo motor capable of precisely controlling its rotation, and an SD card reader for storing the data set locally. To be sure, the device doesn’t log a rider’s location or transmit data; everything operates offline. “I’d say the harder part is actually just building an enclosure that fit perfectly onto the frame that you could just slip on without any additional hardware,” Blinder said. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ground-truth-components-02.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ground-truth-circuit-schematic.png?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ground-truth-device-01.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ground-truth-mainboard.png?quality=90&strip=all] The issue of finding the right housing data to use turned out to be the real challenge. He eventually settled on using the US government’s American Community Survey’s Rent Burden dataset, so as to accurately capture the proportion of a household’s income that was being put toward rent and utilities. Blinder said he uses two measures: the median share of income spent on rent and the percentage of renting households that spend at least half of their income on housing. He then assigns each census block group a value corresponding to the amount of brake tension the device should apply there. Then he took it for a test ride. He found that riding through neighborhoods with a lot of public housing, such as apartment buildings managed by the city’s NYCHA housing agency, the bike would go faster. Meanwhile, some luxury towers are legally required to have affordable apartments, which can complicate the picture presented by those opposed to their construction. His Ground Truth project was already producing surprising results. “So it is sometimes really hard to tell what is affordable, what isn’t,” he said. Blinder said he originally wanted to organize group rides using Citi Bikes, but was unsure whether that would expose him to legal issues. He’s also thinking about how to make Ground Truth more socially interactive as an art project. One possibility is to allow riders to contribute something to the project while they ride. Another would be incorporating additional datasets that could bring different urban or socioeconomic issues into sharper focus. The project could end up evolving significantly in the future. “So it’s really just thinking about what our preconceptions about affordability are,” he said, “and how we can kind of throw a wrench in that at times.” Images by Justin Blinder

articles.title: Trump’s dumb border wall
articles.summary: Border crossings are down. High-tech surveillance is more effective than physical barriers. Still, the Trump administration wants destructive walls anyway.
articles.body: About 22 miles south of the former mining town of Patagonia, Arizona, down a winding, unpaved mountain road that passes cows grazing on open range, stands a cottonwood tree believed to be at least 200 years old. The “grandmother” tree, as some locals call it, is imperiled and already showing signs of stress, almost as if it knows its fate. The leaves are yellowing prematurely, falling to the ground at the height of summer. On July 27th, a construction crew felled three neighboring trees to build an extension of President Donald Trump’s wall along the US-Mexico border. An activist climbed up the last tree standing two days later and ever since, someone has sat on a platform hoisted onto the tree’s branches. They say they’ll sit there as long as it takes, because as long as someone is in the tree, it can’t be cut down. The protest is about more than one cottonwood. “This tree represents a literal line in the sand against border militarization in general,” said Russ McSpadden, the Southwest conservation advocate for the Center for Biological Diversity. In recent weeks, the Department of Homeland Security has revived its effort to wall off the border, dispatching construction crews to remote parts of Texas, Arizona, and the Tohono O’odham Nation’s reservation lands to finish Trump’s wall — and has waived environmental laws to get it built, causing backlash from the tiny desert town of Ajo to the even tinier ghost town of Terlingua. This latest construction push is happening despite record-low encounters along the southwestern border. In fact, encounters at the southwest border dropped almost immediately after Trump took office — not because of any new infrastructure, but because he effectively shut down asylum. Despite the steep decline in migrant crossings, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed along party lines in 2025, gave Trump an additional $46.5 billion to finish building the wall.  The border wall is more than just a wall; it’s a vast surveillance network of interconnected drones, towers, and cameras. Even in areas where there’s no visible barrier separating the United States and Mexico, CBP relies on this “virtual wall” to track migrants. This vast surveillance apparatus is far more effective than a wall, and it’s already largely in place. In the ghost town of Lochiel, Arizona, activists from surrounding communities have set up an encampment on private property near the cottonwood tree to support the protest. They take turns cooking meals and use a pulley system to transport food and water to the person sitting in the tree. They know they’re being watched. Trucks from Vision Quest Solutions, a private security firm that advertises itself as veteran- and Native American-owned, roll up and down the fresh dirt road just south of the tree. The activists track the various contractors that are building the road: Fisher Sand & Gravel, BJ Drilling, Stinger Bridge & Iron, and others. [Image: Homeland Security contractors drive past an ancient cottonwood tree in Lochiel, Arizona. Activists have been occupying the tree since July 29th. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/border_wall_tree_sit_e6f222.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Henry, a community organizer from Tucson who is participating in the encampment, said that a DHS helicopter flew “dangerously close” to the tree on August 10th.  “This movement was started and held down for a long time by local environmentalists who care really deeply about these ancient cottonwood trees,” said Henry, who asked to be referred to by a pseudonym. He is among a newer group of activists “who see it as an opportunity to physically stop border wall construction.” The planned construction projects differ by region. In Arizona’s San Rafael Valley, where an older fence already divides Mexico and the United States, DHS is building a wall featuring 30-foot-tall steel bollards. articles.title: Apple squashes EU beef with new App Store rules
articles.summary: Apple is once again overhauling App Store rules in the European Union, which the company says resolves its disagreements with the European Commission.
articles.body: Apple is once again overhauling App Store rules in the European Union, which the company says will resolve its “disagreements with the Commission over business terms and alternative distribution.” As part of the changes, every developer that distributes apps will be moved to a single set of business terms, and digital transactions for apps distributed outside of the App Store will be subject to a Core Technology Commission fee of 5 percent. The new terms go into effect on October 1st. They will include a 26 percent commission for App Store apps that use Apple’s in-app purchase system, or a 20 percent fee for developers using alternate payment providers. Developers must also pay a 15 percent commission on purchases that link out of the app. Apple will reduce these rates for developers in the App Store Small Business Program, Mini Apps Partner Program, or Video Partner Program. With the new terms, developers can offer both in-app purchases and alternative payment systems in the EU. However, developers must maintain the payment options they choose for 12 months “to provide consistency and clarity for users,” Apple says. There’s also a 5 percent Core Technology Commission on digital transactions in apps distributed on third-party app stores and the web. Apple will no longer charge an initial acquisition fee, store services fee, or the Core Technology Fee, a €0.50 per download fee that applied to apps for each annual install over 1 million.  Web distribution is only available in the EU, Apple says, and the company has eligibility requirements in place for who can actually operate a third-party app marketplace over the web, like being a publicly traded company or having completed a financial audit from a “licensed accountant.” Apple changed its App Store rules last year to comply with the Digital Markets Act (DMA), a set of rules regulating Big Tech. The company has remained critical of the regulations and was fined last year after the Commission found that its App Store “anti-steering” practices violated the DMA. Apple lost its bid to exclude the App Store and iOS from the DMA last month. Apple’s updates also include new child safety features for the EU. Kids apps in the App Store can’t have links to websites for finishing transactions, and Apple won’t let App Store apps link out to websites for a purchase if a user is under 13 years old. Users under 18 will have to get permission from a parent or guardian when trying to make a purchase using an alternative payment method inside an App Store app.

articles.title: Meta glasses are a workplace menace
articles.summary: Meta glasses are quickly becoming a problem in workplaces. Public-facing workers are being filmed, harassed, and creeped out by AI-powered smart glasses.
articles.body: In August, Toru Hinkle was stocking shelves at their job at Target when they noticed two customers and asked if they needed any help. The men requested a price check on an item — but even after Hinkle told them the item was $20, the customers asked for the price again and again.  “After a while, I realized that I’m basically being pranked, and I noticed the glasses,” Hinkle says, referring to the frames with a blinking light. They were the Ray-Ban Meta glasses, and the customers were filming. Hinkle eventually called a store manager over, but the pranksters antagonized her, too — asking the price repeatedly, deliberately misgendering Hinkle as “ma’am” and the female manager as “sir.” At one point, Hinkle attempted to stop the recording by saying “Meta, stop recording” out loud, hoping to trigger a voice control setting. The customers pretended to be confused by the accusation that they were recording Hinkle. The confrontation made Hinkle queasy. “I felt like this pit in my stomach just started to build up,” Hinkle recalls. “After this whole exchange happened, the rest of the shift, I was just quiet and didn’t even talk to anyone because I was just so shaken up by it.” Another customer called the police, Hinkle says, and the two men were escorted out of the store. Target declined to comment. The two customers were, in fact, recording Hinkle, and the entire exchange was turned into content for social media. Another Target manager came across the video while scrolling online, without even looking for it. One clip featuring the incident with Hinkle viewed by The Verge had almost 400,000 views on Instagram and 155,000 views on TikTok. Meta has sold millions of pairs of its AI-powered smart glasses over the last several years — but as sales boom, so too has the backlash to the devices. The glasses allow wearers to listen to music or take calls, but the feature that has sparked outrage is the ability to record using them: Many people see them as a new notch in the surveillance apparatus at best, and “pervert” and “creep” glasses at worst.  Ordinarily, if you are recorded against your will, you can try to leave the area or otherwise resist being recorded. But many people are encountering smart glasses for the first time while at their job, especially those who interact with the public, like retail and service workers. In the workplace, smart glasses exacerbate the power imbalance between the customer and the employee, or the boss and subordinate. Resisting invasive technology is risky when you depend on your job to pay rent or buy groceries. It’s harder still when many workplaces don’t yet have policies around a new gadget that the public is grappling with in real time. Service and retail workers in particular have become a target for stealth — and annoying — smart glasses recording. People wearing Meta glasses are going into stores and harassing or “pranking” employees, using the footage for content and making unwitting workers the butt of the joke. The video made of Hinkle and their manager without their consent is the exact kind of content that Instagram has claimed it will now remove — yet the account that uploaded it was filled with similar “prank” videos harassing workers at their jobs.  There’s little recourse for those who have been unknowingly recorded. articles.title: TikTok will pay $400 million to settle DOJ child privacy lawsuit
articles.summary: The US Department of Justice announced on Friday that TikTok will pay $400 million to settle a lawsuit filed in 2024 over allegedly violating the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA).
articles.body: The US Department of Justice announced on Friday that TikTok will pay $400 million to settle a lawsuit filed in 2024 over allegedly violating the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA). In the lawsuit, the DOJ alleged that TikTok collected data from children without notifying parents or obtaining consent and did not delete the accounts when parents requested. TikTok is set to pay $300 million right away and will pay a further $100 million “upon entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree entered against TikTok’s predecessor, Musical.ly,” the DOJ says in a press release. The settlement is “one of the largest recoveries ever obtained in a COPPA case.” The DOJ also notes that TikTok has “undergone significant changes to its ownership, management, compliance functions, and privacy practices” since the lawsuit was filed and that TikTok has “implemented extensive measures designed to strengthen safeguards for younger users, improve age-related controls, and enhance parental oversight.” TikTok didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. In January, the deal to put TikTok under a new joint ownership structure in the US finally happened.

articles.summary: A Truth Social post landed at the open and immediately sent Detroit's Big Three into a tailspin, but the selloff is hitting Ford and Stellantis twice as hard...
articles.body:
Ford (F) and Stellantis (STLA) each fell 4% after Trump announced 50% tariffs on all Canadian vehicles and parts starting January 2027.

Canada's ambassador Mark Wiseman said the written trade text diverged from what Canada believed it agreed to, collapsing U.S.-Canada talks.

Ford ( NYSE:F ) stock is down 4% to $13.87 in Monday mid-morning trading after President Trump announced a sharp escalation in auto tariffs targeting Canadian imports. Meanwhile, Stellantis ( NYSE:STLA ) shares are also down 4% to $5.19, while General Motors ( NYSE:GM ) stock is down 2% to $86.28.

The selling is sorting within Detroit's Big Three, with Ford and Stellantis taking the harder hit on the tape today. For context, the Global X Autonomous & Electric Vehicles ETF ( NASDAQ:DRIV ) is down 2% to $34.25.

The tariff itself isn't yet in force, and Trump's announced 50% duty on Canadian vehicles and parts is set to take effect January 1, 2027, so Monday's tape is repricing an announced future cost. Ford stock was up 17% year to date through Friday's close, so today's slide erodes a slice of that lead. Stellantis has traded well below year-end levels heading in, which magnifies the sting for shareholders already sitting on losses.

Truth Social Post Triggers the Auto Selloff

In a Truth Social post Monday, Trump wrote, "On January first, 2027, tariffs on all cars, trucks, both large and small, automotive parts, and steel, will be increased to 50%." He accused Canada of "ripping off" the United States and cited a $60 billion trade deficit as justification for the escalation. The post landed at the open of the week and immediately pressured cross-border auto exposure across the Detroit names.

The auto action follows the collapse of U.S.-Canada trade talks late Friday. Separately, Washington applied 50% tariffs to about $20 billion of Canadian goods after talks broke down, 5% of Canada's exports to the U.S., covering electronics, industrial machinery, dairy, paper goods, appliances, and agricultural equipment. That levy is distinct from the forward-dated auto duty, and Canada announced counter-tariffs scheduled to take effect September 8.

Why Talks Collapsed and Where Automakers Fit

Canada's ambassador to the U.S., Mark Wiseman, told Bloomberg that Canada "needed medium and heavy duty vehicles to be included" in any tariff relief, noting the issue directly affects General Motors and Ford, both of which operate assembly in Canada. He stated, "That's just something we could not accept because we want to protect the existence of an automotive assembly industry in Canada for cars, light trucks, you know, medium trucks and heavy-duty trucks."

articles.title: Scott Bessent’s $1 Trillion Bond Market Fight — Treasury Yields Aren’t Buying It
articles.summary: Scott Bessent is sitting on nearly $1 trillion and signaling he will use it to wrestle long-term Treasury yields back down, but the bond market keeps shruggi...
articles.body:
Bessent doubled Treasury buybacks to $4 billion per operation, but the 30-year yield rebounded to 5.247% within 24 hours, erasing all gains.

The TGA's $1 trillion sounds powerful, but usable funds are only somewhere between $100 billion and $200 billion, barely enough to shift the weighted-average maturity of federal debt.

Treasury wants lower long-term yields while the Fed battles inflation, a direct policy collision that could punish the dollar if private investors don't return.

The bond market has become the place where Washington's promises meet hard financial reality. Long-term Treasury yields have climbed as investors demand compensation for inflation, deficits, geopolitical risk, and an enormous supply of government debt.

That makes Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's latest maneuver important for investors well beyond the bond market. Treasury is trying to put a floor under prices at the long end, but the market is making clear that liquidity support is not the same thing as fixing the underlying fiscal math.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Treasury announced that it would at least double the maximum size of its liquidity-support buybacks for 10-to-20-year and 20-to-30-year nominal Treasuries from $2 billion to at least $4 billion per operation. The change begins Sept. 9 and runs through the Nov. 4 quarterly refunding. Treasury says these purchases target older, less-liquid "off-the-run" securities to improve market functioning — not reduce overall federal debt.

The market initially listened. The 30-year yield dropped nearly 10 basis points on Aug. 19 to 5.187%, after reaching 5.337% the previous day, its highest level since 2007. The 10-year yield fell to 4.651%.

Then reality arrived. President Donald Trump warned of an "economic D-Day" against Iran, while oil remained above $90 a barrel. On Aug. 20, the 10-year yield climbed 4.7 basis points to 4.70%, while the 30-year reached 5.247%. Treasury's one-day victory had largely evaporated.

Washington is flooding the market with billions to suppress interest rates, yet yields are still hitting decade highs. It's a high-stakes collision between government intervention and fiscal truth. © 24/7 Wall St.

Bessent subsequently suggested the $4 billion figure could be exceeded. On Aug. 24, Treasury officials indicated the department is considering using its Treasury General Account (TGA), which was approaching $1 trillion, to fund expanded buybacks.

Elon Musk may have left Washington, and the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) may be dead, but the changes the agency helped unleash on Social Security are very much alive.

DOGE officially reached its planned expiration date (1) on July 4, 2026, after shutting down months earlier. The initiative launched sweeping efforts to shrink the federal workforce and overhaul government agencies, with more than 260,000 federal employees leaving government service in 2025 amid layoffs, early retirements, deferred resignations and a hiring freeze.

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

Social Security offers one of the clearest examples of what DOGE left behind.

Nearly 8,000 employees have left (2) the agency since President Donald Trump returned to office, according to Office of Personnel Management data cited by the Federal News Network. The Social Security Administration (SSA) entered 2026 with roughly 50,000 employees, leaving the agency with its smallest workforce in decades, even as it serves around 75 million beneficiaries. Musk himself has since called DOGE only "somewhat successful" and said he wouldn't undertake the effort again.

Yet, Social Security is still moving ahead with an increasingly technology-driven future. Its newly released strategic plan (3) for fiscal years 2026 through 2030 describes its goals as "transformative," with a focus on faster, more reliable service, technology and productivity. That approach builds on changes DOGE pushed at the agency under Musk (4), including workforce reductions, greater reliance on online services and an explicit effort to use technology and automation to improve efficiency.

Can technology make up for thousands of lost workers?

The American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE), which represents SSA workers, says the agency has long been understaffed and under-resourced. The union is calling for Congress to provide roughly $3 billion in additional funding and eventually add 20,000 employees.

The SSA says (5) its modernization push is working. The agency reported that wait times at field offices fell 23% in fiscal 2025 compared with 2024, while its initial disability claims backlog fell 25%.

articles.title: Robotaxis are real now — so is the pushback
articles.summary: Robotaxi companies like Waymo and Zoox are running into obstacles in an increasing number of cities as the fight to shape the rules over driverless operations intensifies.
articles.body: Robotaxis are expanding. So is the fight over the rules governing them. In New York, Gov. Kathy Hochul withdrew a proposal earlier this year that would have opened the door to driverless robotaxis outside New York City after taxi drivers, unions, and state lawmakers opposed it. Six months later, commercial driverless service remains illegal in the state, and legalization efforts are stalled. In DC, labor unions are fighting legislation that would legalize commercial robotaxis, while lawmakers are weighing a 200-vehicle cap and a 15-cent-per-mile fee that would fund Metro upgrades and aid workers displaced by autonomous vehicles. A July City Council hearing on the proposal stretched for a grueling 10 hours. In San Francisco, Mayor Daniel Lurie, a vocal supporter of robotaxis, is now calling for tougher robotaxi regulations after Waymos repeatedly snarled traffic during emergencies and major events. And as of July, California police can now formally cite autonomous-vehicle manufacturers when their driverless cars break traffic laws. And while Congress has yet to pass comprehensive robotaxi legislation, federal regulators have stepped up their scrutiny. The Trump administration’s National Highway Traffic Safety Administration recently warned autonomous-vehicle companies that vehicles unable to safely interact with police, firefighters, and other first responders pose a danger to the public. Even in states that have broadly welcomed autonomous vehicles, governments are grappling with how to oversee them. Texas this year began enforcing new permitting requirements for commercial AV operators, while cities in Florida have complained that state preemption laws leave them with little power to respond to problems on their own streets. Taxi drivers, labor unions, and safety advocates have fought autonomous vehicles for years. What’s changing is the scale and immediacy of the fight. Now that robotaxis have burst free from the pages of science fiction and onto actual city streets, policymakers are confronting a messier reality filled with questions about safety, regulation, growth, and jobs. They’re having to decide how quickly fleets should be allowed to expand, what companies must prove before they do, and how much control cities and states should have over their operations. Waymo, the market leader, is currently operating more than 3,500 vehicles publicly in 11 US cities. Zoox — a purpose-built robotaxi without a steering wheel that bears a striking resemblance to a toaster — just began offering paid rides in Las Vegas and continues to offer free trips to users of its Explorer program in San Francisco as it collects feedback. It’s testing in a total of 10 cities and plans to extend the Explorer program to Austin and Miami later this year. Tesla, which began its Robotaxi rollout with a safety monitor aboard more than a year ago, appears to finally be growing its unsupervised fleet ahead of launching its purpose-built robotaxi, the Cybercab, later this month. Still, for all the political attention, robotaxis remain a tiny share of the US ridehailing market. While Waymo now provides more than 500,000 paid rides a week, Uber handles about 40 million trips a day globally. At that scale, robotaxis haven’t yet displaced many driving jobs or fundamentally changed how cities move. But their visibility vastly exceeds their market share, especially when a driverless car stops in the wrong place during a blackout or interferes with an emergency response. And the consequences could look very different as autonomous fleets grow from thousands of vehicles to hundreds of thousands. That’s why the battles taking shape across the country are increasingly about the terms of expansion: what companies have to prove before they grow, what they owe cities and workers, and how much control cities and states should have over their operations. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/gettyimages-2286668940.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] What the critics want In many places, the robotaxi rollout has outpaced the rules governing it. “Robotaxis are popping up all over the place,” said Shua Sanchez, national campaign director of SAVE-US, a nonprofit advocating for stricter state AV legislation in the absence of federal rules. “The state legislatures don’t have experience with this technology, and there aren’t good laws on the books to regulate them.” SAVE-US is working with lawmakers in New Jersey and New York on a three-pronged approach. It wants multi-stage testing and commercial-deployment permits, under which companies would have to demonstrate their vehicles can operate safely with a small fleet before adding more cars, while continuing to share safety data after commercial service begins. It also wants autonomous vehicles to use multiple kinds of sensors, rather than relying on cameras alone (as Tesla does), and is calling for restrictions on marketing terms like “Autopilot” or “Full Self-Driving” for consumer driver-assist features when the systems still require human oversight. The group isn’t opposed to autonomous vehicles, Sanchez said, but is “pro the safe development of technology.” He added that AV safety isn’t a settled question, and that even a strong record today doesn’t guarantee the same after a software or hardware change. Sen. Ed Markey (D-MA), who has pushed for greater federal oversight of AVs, makes a similar argument about transparency. “Autonomous vehicle companies are making huge claims about how their technology is going to save lives,” Markey told The Verge in a statement. “But right now, our regulatory structure amounts to this: we hope they’re telling the truth.” Markey has investigated AV companies’ use of remote human operators and introduced legislation that would require them to regularly report safety data. "“Right now, our regulatory structure amounts to this: we hope they’re telling the truth.”" - Sen. Ed Markey “Communities deserve transparency and consistent oversight before we let Big Tech invade their public roads,” he said. But safety is only part of the fight. For labor groups, the stakes are also economic. Peter Finn, Teamsters international vice president at large, called autonomous vehicles an “existential threat” to the work his members do. He pointed to the enormous number of jobs potentially affected by autonomous driving beyond rideshare drivers, including truckers, delivery drivers, and other commercial drivers. Like other groups in the robotaxi debate, the Teamsters insist they aren’t opposed to new technology in principle. But that still leaves them staking out positions that would sharply constrain how autonomous vehicles are deployed.  That includes requiring heavy-duty autonomous vehicles like semitrucks to have a trained human operator aboard — legislation the Teamsters have twice pushed in California, only to see Gov. Gavin Newsom veto it. Finn said the Teamsters plan to pursue the issue again. “If the technology is solely designed to automate and eliminate labor costs, the only entity benefiting from that is corporations,” Finn said. The Teamsters’ immediate legislative priority isn’t robotaxis themselves so much as what it sees coming next. To Finn, Waymo and Zoox are precursors to a much larger fight over autonomous driving. He pointed specifically to Zoox’s ownership by Amazon, arguing that similar technology could eventually be applied to package delivery. Zoox and Waymo both said their current focus remains their robotaxi services. Taken together, the objections go beyond any one safety rule or labor concern. AV resistance has become part of a broader backlash to Big Tech’s growing physical footprint, from data centers to Flock cameras. Companies are pouring enormous sums into new infrastructure, and many residents are still asking what, exactly, they get in return for having it in their communities. [Image: Tesla Cybercabs are lined up on a lot at Tesla Giga Texas in Austin, Wednesday, April 8th. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/gettyimages-2270749488.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Even robotaxi companies want rules Robotaxi companies, meanwhile, are trying to get ahead of the backlash — and sidestep a patchwork of confusing state and local laws — by helping shape the rules themselves. That includes supporting certain regulations while pushing back on others they see as too restrictive. “I want to unequivocally say we agree with the administrator and the administration and the regulatory agency. We need to be regulated,” Zoox CEO Aicha Evans recently said on Fox Business in response to NHTSA’s warnings about unsafe interactions with emergency vehicles. Zoox said it is also trying to head off conflicts before entering new markets. Ron Thaniel, the company’s senior director of policy and regulatory affairs, said Zoox establishes lines of communication with local and state officials and conducts hands-on engagement with first responders before launching in a city. As the industry expands, he said, Zoox sees “an opportunity at the federal level to more uniformly regulate autonomous vehicles.” Waymo told The Verge much the same thing. “I think there definitely needs to be some regulation,” Waymo global head of public policy Justin Kintz said. “They’re powered by incredible technology that makes the world a safer place, but it still needs oversight from the federal government, from states, and from cities in the same way that they manage human drivers today.” "“I want to unequivocally say we agree with the administrator and the administration and the regulatory agency. We need to be regulated.”" - Zoox CEO Aicha Evans Zoox and Waymo are hardly alone in wanting clearer rules. The Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association, which counts both companies as members, has said only about half of US states have passed laws that allow vehicles to operate without humans. The industry group believes states should establish a legal framework for AVs, require first-responder interaction plans, and set minimum requirements before vehicles can operate without a human driver. (The association didn’t respond to requests for more specifics.) Waymo said it has long advocated for a national AV safety standard covering minimum testing requirements, vehicle design, and data sharing. Under its preferred system, the federal government would continue setting vehicle safety standards, while states would govern road rules and cities would handle local concerns like curb space, law enforcement, and emergency response. The disagreements emerge in the details. In Washington, DC, Waymo said it broadly supports Councilmember Charles Allen’s effort to establish a regulatory framework allowing commercial robotaxi service, including its goals of funding transit and helping workers transition as transportation becomes more automated. But it objects to parts of the current proposal. Waymo said a 200-vehicle limit would probably be too small for a city the size of Washington. It could accept starting small, but wants regulators to let fleets grow as companies demonstrate safe performance rather than putting a permanent ceiling into law. “I don’t think legislation needs to set a hard cap on that,” Kintz said, “or it’s going to lead to preventing important groups from being able to access the service when they need it.” The company has been more receptive to the proposed 15-cent fee for every mile an autonomous vehicle travels. Kintz said Waymo supports “the fundamental principle of raising revenue” for transit and affected workers, though it raised concerns that a per-mile charge could become prohibitively expensive, particularly for smaller AV operators. An annual fee, it suggested, is one possible alternative. Emergency response is another area where Waymo says it supports regulation, even as it argues that some of the work is already underway. After NHTSA called for stronger coordination between AV companies and first responders, Waymo said it immediately asked to participate in the agency’s discussions. The company said it already maintains dedicated first responder training programs and 24/7 priority lines for dispatchers and officers, while Kintz acknowledged that “we haven’t always got it right.” "“We haven’t always got it right.”" - Waymo global head of public policy Justin Kintz Waymo is also trying to make the case that robotaxis can complement, rather than undermine, public transit. In a Streetsblog piece this month, Waymo policy development and research manager Arielle Fleisher argued the company has “common cause” with urbanists trying to reduce dependence on private cars. A July City Council hearing on the proposal stretched for a grueling 10 hours. In San Francisco, Mayor Daniel Lurie, a vocal supporter of robotaxis, is now calling for tougher robotaxi regulations after Waymos repeatedly snarled traffic during emergencies and major events. And as of July, California police can now formally cite autonomous-vehicle manufacturers when their driverless cars break traffic laws. The Trump administration’s National Highway Traffic Safety Administration recently warned autonomous-vehicle companies that vehicles unable to safely interact with police, firefighters, and other first responders pose a danger to the public. articles.title: The cat-and-mouse game over 3D-printed guns has begun
articles.summary: The ‘Hochulization’ tool purports to subvert proposed gun-blocking 3D printer software.
articles.body: The creator of the world’s first 3D-printed gun claims he’s developed a way to thwart government-mandated software meant to block 3D printers from making firearms. It’s an opening volley in what’s shaping up to be an evolving battle between regulators trying to stem the tide of ghost guns and individuals trying to create workarounds. Cody Wilson, who claims to have made the detection-defying tool, is calling it “Hochulization” as a direct jab at New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, who pushed through the nation’s first law mandating gun file detection software on new printers earlier this year. “New York is trying to reach into the internet and police how open-source 3D printing is done,” Wilson, who’s based out of Austin, Texas, told The Verge. “I think of it as a self-defense measure.” The tool is designed to break a relatively simple approach to a 3D-printed gun ban. Wilson’s company, Defense Distributed, runs DEFCAD, the world’s largest 3D gun file repository, which he says hosts over 200,000 files of gun designs and components, such as suppressors. Each of those files can be identified by a hash, a unique string of numbers that’s created by running the file through an algorithm. In theory, a gun file detection system that uses a hashing-based identification method would look for those exact hashes to determine whether a file is a potential gun, flag it, and prevent it from printing. Hochulization mucks up that process by automatically changing those hashes. It adds a series of bytes to each file that changes the hash without altering the function of the end product. A 3D-printed suppressor or gun, in other words, would still work as intended. “Hochulizaiton is a de minimis policy to change the hash of every file that gets created and downloaded to where there is never going to be a complete library of hashes,” Wilson says. Wilson says he wants to apply the Hochulization treatment to all files hosted on DEFCAD by default as a means of “self-defense” against growing calls for gun detection software, which he describes as invasive digital surveillance. Wilson says he will make the tool available to DEFCAD users, though he says he also intends to make it open source, which would let an individual user with a gun file apply the tool to scramble the hash and potentially sidestep detection. [Image: Image: Cody Wilson https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_9601.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] “I think all the files in the repository, the 3D files anyway, should be Hochulized,” he adds. “And so that is what we’ll do.” He claims he has begun this process. Wilson’s approach is an early indicator of the resistance to 3D-print-blocking tech. In this case, the momentum is coming from a Second Amendment advocate, but that might not always be the case. Groups of makers, digital rights experts, and members of the entertainment industry who aren’t focused on guns have all spoken out against the tech, expressing fears that requiring file scanning on printers introduces a new level of digital surveillance into the process that could limit what everyone can create. 3D-printed firearms are growing in number but remain an evolving public threat. In 2021, the New York Police Department confiscated just one 3D-printed gun. That jumped to 109 in 2024. Prominent gun policy group Everytown found similar upticks across 20 other cities. Still, when compared with the percentage of conventional firearms confiscated around the country, 3D-printed models remain comparatively small. The total number of firearms in the US has been estimated to outnumber people. But 3D-printed gun technology has also come a long way since Wilson first printed his single-shot “Liberator” in 2013. Today, models like the FGC-9 can fire multiple high-velocity rounds without breaking and have been found in the hands of neo-Nazi cells in Europe and rebel groups fighting Myanmar’s military junta. 3D-printed gun components, like switches that can turn a single-fire conventional firearm into a machine gun or suppressors that make shots easier to conceal, are arguably even more dangerous. These tools are typically illegal or require special licenses to acquire. 3D printing offers a workaround. Luigi Mangione, who admitted to shooting and killing UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson and is awaiting sentencing, allegedly used a partially 3D-printed Glock-style pistol frame and a 3D-printed suppressor. Policymakers and gun control advocates argue cases like this demonstrate a glaring gap in the legal system. People with prior felony convictions and others who aren’t legally allowed to own guns can do so anyway with the help of a 3D printer. And while many states regulate the making and selling of so-called “ghost guns,” actually enforcing those laws is notoriously difficult. This new approach, which requires 3D printers to install mandatory file-blocking software, attempts to close that gap by stopping a print before it ever starts. Industry experts are still debating whether that’s technically feasible at scale. Gov. Hochul, who pushed through the country’s first law mandating print-blocking software on new printers as part of the state’s FY 2027 budget, says it’s necessary to close what she calls a black-market “plastic pipeline.” Hochul’s office did not respond to our request for comment regarding Wilson’s Hochulization workaround. New York isn’t alone. A similar bill in California, AB 2047, is gaining momentum and is advancing to the Senate floor for a vote. Like in New York, this bill would require new printers manufactured or sold in the state to be equipped with print-blocking software. The state Department of Justice would publish a roster of compliant printer models, and those not on the list would be banned from sale or transfer in the state starting in December 2029. A spokesperson for California Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, who introduced and coauthored AB 2047, declined to comment when asked about Wilson’s project. Neither of these efforts explicitly details what print-blocking software should look like. That’s being left up to groups of industry experts with backgrounds in manufacturing technology, artificial intelligence, firearms regulation, and other relevant fields. A purely hash-matching approach would limit the number of non-guns mistakenly identified as guns, but as Wilson’s project shows, it may be trivially easy to bypass. More expansive approaches that use AI to analyze a file’s geometry and predict whether it’s a gun would almost certainly prevent more guns from being printed, but they also risk introducing more false positives. Wilson’s hoping his tool will make its way into those working group conversations. By showing just how simple it is to complicate a purely hashing-based approach, he’s essentially trying to force policymakers’ hands into choosing between a more aggressive scanning scheme or the status quo of nothing.  “You are going to have to do more than create a database of known files and check against hashes because that’s too easy to defeat,” Wilson says.  Dartmouth College associate professor of engineering Solomon Diamond told The Verge Hochulization would likely work on a technical level to bypass a hash-based detection model. Still, he said that doesn’t necessarily make the approach useless as a policy path. In reality, it’s not clear that every 3D printer user would go the extra step to change a hash. Downloading gun files from DEFCAD also requires setting up an account and linking an email address, which is another barrier to entry. The hashing approach, in other words, is better than nothing and might stop the casual, less motivated user from downloading a gun. Moving beyond hash matching, Wilson says his team found other ways to bypass more sophisticated detection using “adversarial noise.” To do this, his team first created their own AI detection model designed to classify guns and gun parts, trained partly on both public and non-public files from DEFCAD’s database. They based their model on claims made by other companies, such as the Spain-based Print&Go, which is working with lawmakers in New York and California. Wilson claims he was able to get files past their own system using techniques like re-saving the same gun part as a slightly different mesh (a digital representation of the object’s surface) or adding “a small extra lump of unused geometry.” Overall, Wilson says their gun detection system, even when trained on high-quality data, still had a 30 percent false positive rate. He says that false positives speak to issues inherent to more prediction-based systems.  Wilson approaches the scanning debate as a self-described crypto-anarchist and an aggressive Second Amendment advocate. He’s a leading voice in arguing that gun files should be considered constitutionally protected speech under the First Amendment. He also created the platform Hatreon as an alternative to Patreon to thwart its speech policies, a platform that attracted extremists, white supremacists, and neo-Nazis until it was shut down in 2018. But concerns over this proposed change to the way 3D printing works aren’t limited to gun owners. Makers and hobbyists previously told The Verge they fear this new paradigm will falsely label non-guns, like this e-reader case, as dangerous weapons and limit their freedom of expression in the process. Others are concerned a process that earnestly starts with gun file increments could be expanded by corporations looking to enforce IP and copyright protections. Wilson isn’t new when it comes to picking fights over 3D-printed gun laws. After posting the first Liberator files online, the State Department ordered him to remove them and threatened him with jail time for allegedly violating ITAR export-control rules. Wilson and Defense Distributed sued the agency, claiming they attempted to stop him from publishing computer code, which he says is constitutionally protected under the First Amendment. That set in motion a complex web of legal fights over the broad claim that the gun file codes aren’t constitutionally protected speech, an issue that’s still being debated in courts.

Robert Kiyosaki has never been shy about issuing dire financial warnings. But with America's national debt reaching a staggering new milestone, the Rich Dad Poor Dad author is turning up the volume.

"$40 TRILLION US NATIONAL [debt] soon!!" Kiyosaki wrote (1) on X. "What are you doing about it?"
